question.prompt: Given the progression \[ \begin{gathered} 10^{\frac{1}{11}},10^{\frac{2}{11}},10^{\frac{3}{11}},\\ 10^{\frac{4}{11}},\ldots,10^{\frac{n}{11}}, \end{gathered} \] the least positive integer \(n\) such that the product of the first \(n\) terms exceeds \(100{,}000\) is:

solutions.explanation:
Each term \(10^{k/11}\), for positive integer \(k\), is greater than \(1\). Thus the products of the first \(n\) terms strictly increase as \(n\) increases.

Among the first ten factors, pair the first with the tenth, the second with the ninth, and so on. Each pair has indices adding to \(11\), so for \(1\le k\le5\),
\[
10^{k/11}\,10^{(11-k)/11}=10^1=10.
\]
The five pairs therefore give a product of \(10^5=100{,}000\). This equals the threshold and does not exceed it. Every earlier partial product is smaller.

The eleventh term is \(10^{11/11}=10\), making the product of the first eleven terms \(10^6\), which exceeds the threshold. Hence the least index is \(\boxed{11}\), choice \(\mathrm{E}\).
solutions.title: Pair factors whose exponents add to one
